outline.description: An overview of sequence‐level modeling, touching on the historical rise of recurrent neural networks, why the Long Short‑Term Memory became foundational in NLP, how Transformers displaced them at scale, and finally posing the research question addressed by the paper.
subtopics: Evolution from vanilla RNNs → gated units → Transformers
Why large language models historically relied upon recurrent cores
"Open question" – Can modernised LSTMs reach Transformer‐style performance?
High‐level contributions presented in this work
"Constant error carousel" formulation defining cell and hidden state updates
Three multiplicative gates ‑ input, forget and output ‑ including their activation functions
Vectorisation into multiple cell banks enabling recurrent weight matrices
Recent findings confirming every component’s necessity
"Revision limitation" illustrated through a nearest‑neighbor lookup task that ordinary LSTMs fail because their stored value cannot be updated when a closer match appears later.
"Capacity limitation" shown via rare‑token perplexity analysis where scalar cell states hinder memorising infrequent events.
"Parallelisation barrier" caused by hidden‑to‑hidden recurrences forcing strictly sequential execution.
"Why exponentials" – providing full unit‐range connectivity unlike saturating sigmoids.
(i) Input gate i_exp = exp(ẋ_i); (ii) Forget gate alternative either sigmoid or exp.
(iii) Normaliser n_t accumulates weighted future forget values ensuring comparable scales.
(iv) Stabilise drift via log‑based maximum state m_t preventing overflow while preserving gradients.
